scenarios.title: What Is an IDP?
scenarios.situation: Leadership asks what an Internal Developer Platform actually is, versus 'we have Kubernetes and CI'.
choices: An IDP is the curated set of tools, APIs, and workflows a platform team provides so developers can self-serve infrastructure (environments, deploys, databases) without deep infra expertise — Kubernetes and CI are building blocks, the IDP is the productized layer on top
An IDP is a second Kubernetes cluster reserved for the platform team
An IDP is just a rebranded CI/CD pipeline with a dashboard
An IDP replaces developers; it auto-writes application code
scenarios.why: The distinction is product thinking: raw Kubernetes + CI is a toolkit requiring expertise; an IDP packages them into self-service golden paths with sensible defaults. The platform team treats developers as customers, reducing cognitive load. A cluster alone or a pipeline alone is not a platform.
scenarios.hint: What's the difference between handing someone lumber and handing them a furnished room?

scenarios.title: Catalog Before Automation
scenarios.situation: The platform team wants to build a Backstage-style software catalog but can't agree on what goes in it. Half the services have no owner listed anywhere.
scenarios.prompt: What is the minimum viable catalog entry?
choices: For every component: a name, an owner (team or individual), its lifecycle stage, and links to repo/runbook — ownership and findability come before rich metadata; you can enrich later
Full dependency graphs, API specs, and cost data for every service on day one
Only production services; dev and staging services don't need cataloging
The catalog should list infrastructure (clusters, VPCs) instead of software components
scenarios.why: A catalog's core job is answering 'what is this, who owns it, where is it in its lifecycle, where do I find it.' Ownership is the highest-value field — during incidents, 'who owns this' matters more than anything. Starting with the minimal schema gets adoption; demanding complete metadata up front stalls the project.
scenarios.hint: During a 2 AM incident on an unknown service, which single field would you want most?

scenarios.title: Golden Path vs Wild West
scenarios.situation: Teams each built their own deploy pipeline: 14 variants of 'build, test, push, deploy'. The platform team proposes one blessed 'golden path' pipeline. Teams fear losing flexibility.
scenarios.prompt: How should the platform team position the golden path?
choices: Offer the golden path as the default paved road (supported, secure, maintained) while allowing escape hatches for justified exceptions — adoption comes from making the right way the easy way, not from mandates
Mandate the golden path for all teams immediately; uniformity beats autonomy
Abandon the golden path; 14 pipelines is healthy diversity
Make the golden path maximally configurable so it can replicate all 14 variants
scenarios.why: Golden paths work through attraction, not coercion: teams adopt the paved road because it's faster and maintained, and the platform team learns from the escape-hatch cases. Mandates breed shadow IT; infinite configurability recreates the 14 variants inside one template. The paved-road-with-exits model balances standardization and autonomy.
scenarios.hint: Do people use highways because they're forced to, or because they're the fastest maintained route — with exits available?

scenarios.title: Template Sprawl
scenarios.situation: The platform's software templates (scaffolding) have grown to 40 near-identical 'new service' templates. Maintenance is crushing the platform team.
scenarios.prompt: What is the right consolidation move?
choices: Consolidate to a few parameterized templates (language × workload type) with clear versioning and deprecation of the rest — templates are products with a maintenance cost, and 40 variants means 40 things to patch on every CVE
Keep all 40; choice is good for developers
Delete all templates and let teams copy-paste from existing repos
Auto-generate a template per existing service so coverage is complete
scenarios.why: Every template is a maintenance liability: dependency bumps, security patches, and best-practice updates multiply across variants. A small set of parameterized templates (with inputs for the real variations) gives coverage without the combinatorial burden. Deprecation with migration guides moves teams off the long tail.
scenarios.hint: When the next critical CVE hits a base image, how many places will you have to patch?

scenarios.title: Platform API Design
scenarios.situation: The platform team exposes a 'provision database' API. Team A's request returns in 2 seconds; team B's identical request hangs for 20 minutes then fails with no useful error.
scenarios.prompt: What API design principle was violated?
choices: Long-running operations must be asynchronous with status polling (202 + operation ID + status endpoint) and structured, actionable errors — synchronous 20-minute requests hit timeouts everywhere and opaque errors leave callers helpless
Database provisioning should be synchronous; the bug is just a slow backend
The API needs GraphQL; REST cannot express provisioning operations
Errors should return HTTP 200 with an error body so clients don't retry
scenarios.why: Platform APIs wrap operations that take minutes: the correct pattern is accept-and-track (202 Accepted, operation resource, pollable status, webhooks/events on completion). Synchronous designs collapse under proxies, client timeouts, and retries. And errors must be machine-actionable (codes, remediation hints), because the caller is usually automation, not a human reading logs.
scenarios.hint: What happens to an HTTP request that takes 20 minutes, hop by hop? What should the API have returned in second 1?

scenarios.title: Measuring Platform Success
scenarios.situation: The platform team ships features constantly, but engineering leadership asks: 'Is the platform actually helping?' DORA metrics for product teams are flat.
scenarios.prompt: What should the platform team measure?
choices: Developer productivity outcomes: time-to-first-deploy for new services, self-service adoption rate, reduction in infra-related support tickets, and product-team DORA trends for onboarded teams — platform success is measured in developer outcomes, not platform-team output
Number of platform features shipped per quarter; output proves value
Platform team sprint velocity and story points completed
Total lines of Terraform the platform team maintains
scenarios.why: Platforms are force multipliers: their value shows up in the productivity of their users, not their own activity metrics. Time-to-first-commit-to-prod, ticket deflection, and adoption of golden paths directly measure whether the platform reduces friction. Feature counts and velocity measure busyness, and can even be inversely correlated with good platform design (less surface, more leverage).
scenarios.hint: Who is the customer of the platform — and whose numbers should improve if the platform is working?

lessons.title: Platform Engineering — Core concepts
concepts: An Internal Developer Platform is a product: curated tools, APIs, and workflows that let developers self-serve infrastructure. Kubernetes and CI are building blocks; the IDP is the productized layer with developers as customers.
The software catalog is the platform's front door. Minimum viable entry: name, owner, lifecycle stage, repo and runbook links — ownership first, rich metadata later.

Golden paths are paved roads, not mandates: the blessed way to build, test, and ship, maintained and secure by default, with escape hatches for justified exceptions. Adoption comes from being the easiest path.
Software templates scaffold new services consistently, but each template is a maintenance liability — consolidate to a few parameterized templates with versioning and deprecation.
Platform APIs wrap slow operations asynchronously: 202 Accepted with an operation ID, pollable status, and structured actionable errors — because the caller is usually automation.

example.code:
curl -s https://platform.example.com/api/v1/templates | jq '.[].name'
curl -s -X POST https://platform.example.com/api/v1/environments \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"service": "checkout", "type": "preview"}' | jq .operation_id
example.walkthrough: Discover available templates, then request an ephemeral preview environment asynchronously — the API returns an operation ID immediately and you poll for completion instead of holding a 20-minute HTTP connection.

pitfalls: Common trap: measuring platform success by features shipped — measure developer outcomes (time-to-deploy, ticket deflection, adoption).
Common trap: mandating the golden path — mandates breed shadow IT; make it the easiest path instead.
Common trap: 40 near-identical templates — every template multiplies CVE patch work.
Common trap: synchronous platform APIs for minute-long operations — proxies and clients will time out.
lessons.try_it: Work through this in the Labs tab.

labs.title: Catalog Your First Service
labs.objective: Register a service in a Backstage-style software catalog with ownership and lifecycle metadata.
steps: Write a `catalog-info.yaml` (Component kind) with name, description, lifecycle (`production`), and owner.
Define the owner as a `Group` entity (team name, members) referenced by the component.
Add annotations: repo URL, runbook link, and techdocs ref.
Validate the YAML structure (required fields: apiVersion, kind, metadata, spec).
Register it in the catalog UI/API and search for it by owner — confirm ownership is queryable.

checks.hint: The file should declare a Component entity.
Ownership must be present in the metadata or spec.

labs.title: Ship a Golden-Path Template
labs.objective: Build one parameterized software template that scaffolds a production-ready service skeleton.
steps: Define template parameters: service name, language (node/python), and workload type (api/worker).
Write the skeleton: Dockerfile (multi-stage, non-root), k8s manifests with probes and resource requests, CI pipeline stub.
Add template metadata: title, description, owner, and tags for catalog discoverability.
Scaffold two different services from the same template and diff the outputs — only parameters should differ.
Write a deprecation note for one legacy template this new one replaces.

checks.hint: The scaffolded output should include a Dockerfile.
The template definition should declare its parameters.

simulations.title: The platform nobody uses
simulations.brief: The platform team shipped a beautiful IDP with 40 services. Adoption: 3 teams out of 25. The other 22 ship the old way — or with shadow tooling. Diagnose the adoption failure.

steps.symptom: IDP launched 8 months ago. Adoption: 3 of 25 teams. Shadow pipelines: 11 and counting.
evidence: Teams on platform: 3. Teams on legacy Jenkins: 11. Shadow tooling: 11.
'The golden path takes longer than our current way.' (19 teams)
options: The golden path isn't the easiest path — adoption comes from being easier than the alternative, not from mandates
Mandate the platform for all 25 teams immediately
The 22 teams are resistant to change — escalate to their managers
Build more platform features to attract users
steps.explain: An Internal Developer Platform is a product with developers as customers: golden paths are paved roads, not mandates. If the blessed way is slower than the old way, teams route around it — adoption comes from being the easiest path, period.

steps.symptom: The platform requires 14 form fields and 3 approvals to scaffold a service. The old way: one Jenkinsfile.
evidence: New service: 14 fields, 3 approvals, 2-5 day wait. Old way: copy Jenkinsfile, 10 minutes.
options: Reduce the scaffolding friction to beat the 10-minute alternative — every field and approval is a tax on adoption
The fields are necessary for governance — teams must adapt
Add a tutorial explaining why the fields matter
Hide the old Jenkins — remove the alternative
steps.explain: The platform competes with the status quo on every interaction: 14 fields and 3 approvals versus a 10-minute copy is a competition the platform loses. Each required field must justify itself against the adoption it costs.

steps.symptom: The 3 adopted teams love the platform — but they're the platform team's friends from a previous project.
evidence: Adopted: teams A, B, C — all previously worked with platform engineers.
Team D: 'We asked for help twice, got docs links. We stopped asking.'
options: Treat developer support as the product: office hours, pairing, and migration help — the platform team sells outcomes, not docs
The 3 teams prove the platform works — the rest will come
Docs links are sufficient support for senior engineers
Team D is a special case — ignore the outlier
steps.explain: Platform as product means developer support is the product: the teams that adopted had relationships, the ones that didn't got docs links. Office hours, pairing on migrations, and treating friction reports as bugs — that's the adoption engine.

simulations.debrief: Platform adoption is earned: the golden path must be the easiest path, scaffolding friction must beat the alternative, and developer support is the product. Mandates and features don't adopt platforms — outcomes do.

simulations.title: Template sprawl
simulations.brief: The software catalog lists 47 service templates. Half are unmaintained, 6 do the same thing, and new teams pick at random. Consolidate.

steps.symptom: 47 templates in the catalog. Maintained: 23. Duplicates: 6 web-service variants. Usage: scattered.
evidence: New team survey: 'We picked one at random. They all looked the same.'
options: Consolidate to a few parameterized templates with versioning and deprecation — each template is a maintenance liability
More templates means more choice — add the missing variants
Let teams maintain their own templates — decentralize
Delete templates at random until the number looks reasonable
steps.explain: Each template is a maintenance liability: 47 templates means 47 things to patch, secure, and update. Consolidate to a few parameterized templates with versioning and a deprecation path — choice without curation is just confusion.

steps.symptom: Consolidation proposed: 4 templates. Three teams protest — their variant has 'essential' differences.
evidence: Variant differences: port numbers, env var names, label conventions. No architectural differences.
'Our variant is essential because our deploy scripts expect port 8081.'
options: Parameterize the real differences (ports, names) and standardize the rest — essential means architectural, not habitual
Keep all variants — the teams know their needs
Force the 4 templates with no parameters — standardization above all
Let the protesting teams fork the platform
steps.explain: Parameterized templates absorb legitimate variation (ports, names, labels) while standardizing the architecture. 'Essential' differences that are just habits become parameters; the rest converges. Forking recreates the sprawl.

steps.symptom: 4 templates shipped with versioning. Now teams pin to v1 forever and never take updates.
evidence: Teams on template v1: 18. Current: v3. Security fixes in v2, v3: unapplied by 18 teams.
options: Publish a deprecation policy with timelines: old versions get security fixes for N months, then retire
Force-upgrade everyone to v3 overnight
Support v1 forever — stability is a feature
Security fixes aren't critical for templates
steps.explain: Templates need versioning and deprecation: without a sunset policy, every version lives forever and security fixes never land. A published timeline (security fixes for N months, then retire) makes upgrades a planned event, not a surprise.

simulations.debrief: Templates are products with lifecycles: consolidate to a few parameterized ones, version them, and deprecate on a published timeline. Unmaintained choice is worse than constrained choice.

simulations.title: The synchronous platform API
simulations.brief: The platform's provisioning API takes 90 seconds to create an environment — and times out half the calls. CI jobs hang, retries double-provision, and teams are building workarounds. Redesign the API contract.

steps.symptom: POST /environments takes 90s, times out at 60s in most clients. Retries create duplicate environments.
evidence: p50: 88s, p99: 140s. Client timeout: 60s. Duplicates from retries: 23 this month.
Handler: synchronous — provisions everything before responding. No idempotency key.
options: Make provisioning asynchronous: 202 Accepted with an operation ID, pollable status, idempotent retries
Increase all client timeouts to 180s
Make provisioning faster — 90s is the real problem
Tell teams not to retry
steps.explain: Platform APIs wrap slow operations asynchronously: 202 Accepted with an operation ID and pollable status, because the caller is usually automation. Idempotency keys make retries safe — the duplicate environments came from retrying a non-idempotent synchronous call.

steps.symptom: Async API shipped. Now failures surface as 'operation failed' with no detail — automation can't tell retryable from fatal.
evidence: Operation status: 'failed'. Reason: null. Retry policy: blind retry 3x.
Blind retries of fatal errors: 140 this month. Each provisions partial infra.
options: Return structured, actionable errors: machine-readable codes distinguishing retryable, fatal, and needs-input states
'Failed' is enough — humans can check the logs
Retry everything 10 times to be sure
Never fail operations — always return success
steps.explain: The caller is usually automation, so errors must be machine-actionable: structured codes for retryable vs fatal vs needs-input. 'Failed' with no reason forces blind retries — which is how partial infrastructure accumulates.

steps.symptom: The API is solid now, but every team wraps it differently — 9 client libraries, 4 of them broken.
evidence: 'Which client should we use?' — no canonical answer.
options: Ship and support one official client per ecosystem — the API contract includes its clients
Clients are the teams' problem — the API is documented
Ban custom clients
Deprecate the API — clients are too hard
steps.explain: A platform API's contract includes its clients: one official, supported client per ecosystem beats nine divergent wrappers. The API is the product — and products ship SDKs, not just docs.

simulations.debrief: Platform APIs are built for automation: async with operation IDs, idempotent, structured actionable errors, and official clients. The API is a product — design it like one.

simulations.title: Catalog with no owners
simulations.brief: The software catalog has 300 entries. 90 have no owner, 40 point at archived repos, and the 'runbook' links 404. The catalog is where services go to be forgotten. Fix it.

steps.symptom: 300 catalog entries. Owner missing: 90. Repo archived: 40. Runbook links dead: 61.
evidence: Entries: 300. owner: null on 90. repo archived: 40. runbook 404: 61.
Catalog lookups during incidents: 12% of incidents. 'We use Slack instead.'
options: Make ownership the minimum viable entry: no owner, no catalog entry — then enforce freshness with automation
More metadata fields will fix the catalog
Delete the catalog — Slack works fine
Hire someone to manually curate all 300 entries
steps.explain: The software catalog is the platform's front door, and ownership is the minimum viable entry: name, owner, lifecycle stage, repo and runbook links. A catalog that accepts ownerless entries becomes a write-only archive — enforce the minimum at write time.

steps.symptom: Ownership enforced for new entries. The 90 ownerless legacy entries remain — nobody claims them.
evidence: 90 ownerless entries. Claim campaign: 12 claimed, 78 silent.
3 of the 78 run in production. Nobody knows who deploys them.
options: Escalate the unclaimed production services: they get owners by deadline or they get sunset plans — unknown production ownership is a risk
Leave the 78 — they work fine without owners
Assign them all to the platform team
Delete all 78 immediately
steps.explain: Unowned production services are an operational risk with no accountable party. The campaign needs teeth: claim by deadline or the service gets a sunset plan. Assigning them all to the platform team just moves the fiction.

steps.symptom: Catalog is clean. Now entries rot again within months — repos move, owners leave, links die.
evidence: 6 months after cleanup: 34 entries stale again. Owner departures: 11.
Freshness process: quarterly manual review (never happened twice).
options: Automate freshness: sync from the repo, flag stale entries, and nudge owners — curation must be continuous, not quarterly
Do the manual review properly this time
Accept rot — catalogs are snapshots
Lock entries so they can't go stale
steps.explain: Catalogs rot because the world moves: owners leave, repos migrate. Manual quarterly reviews don't happen; automation does — sync ownership from the org chart, validate links continuously, and nudge owners when entries decay. Ownership first, rich metadata later, freshness always.

simulations.debrief: A catalog is a living system: ownership as the price of entry, teeth behind the cleanup, and automated freshness forever. The front door only works if someone maintains the building.

simulations.title: The escape hatch that became the road
simulations.brief: The golden path has an escape hatch for 'justified exceptions.' 60% of new services now use the hatch. The paved road is empty. Reclaim the golden path.

steps.symptom: Escape-hatch usage: 60% of new services. Golden path: 40%. The hatch was meant for rare exceptions.
evidence: New services: 60% escape hatch, 40% golden path. Hatch justifications: mostly blank.
'The golden path didn't support our database.' 'The hatch was faster.'
options: Treat hatch usage as product feedback: find out what the golden path lacks, fix it, and require real justification for the hatch
Remove the escape hatch — everyone on the golden path
The hatch is popular — make it the new golden path
Ignore it — 40% adoption is fine
steps.explain: Golden paths are paved roads, not mandates — but a 60% escape rate is the users voting with their feet. Each hatch use is feedback about what the paved road lacks; fix the road, and require genuine justification (reviewed, expiring) for the exceptions that remain.

steps.symptom: The top hatch reason: the golden path doesn't support the team's database. It never will — it's exotic.
evidence: Database: legacy proprietary, 2 services, no managed offering. Golden path: Postgres or MySQL.
Adding it to the golden path: 3 months of platform work for 2 services.
options: Keep it as a governed exception: documented, reviewed, expiring — not every snowflake belongs on the paved road
Add it to the golden path regardless of cost
Force the 2 services onto Postgres
Remove the database from the platform entirely
steps.explain: Escape hatches exist for justified exceptions — a legacy proprietary database for 2 services is exactly that. The answer is governed exception (documented, reviewed, expiring), not paving the road to every snowflake or forcing a migration that destroys value.

steps.symptom: Hatch usage is down to 8% with real justifications. Now platform leadership wants to report '100% golden path' by closing the hatch.
evidence: Hatch: 8%, all justified and expiring. Golden path: 92%.
'Can we get to 100% for the board slide?'
options: Keep the governed hatch: 100% is a vanity metric, and closing the hatch recreates shadow tooling
Close the hatch — 100% looks better
Report 100% and keep the hatch quietly
The 8% are failures — fix them
steps.explain: A governed 8% exception rate is the healthy steady state — it means the road serves 92% and the exceptions are visible and expiring. Chasing 100% for a slide recreates the shadow tooling the platform was built to replace. Report the honest number.

simulations.debrief: Golden paths need governed escape hatches: the hatch rate is product feedback, genuine exceptions get documented expiry, and 92% with honesty beats 100% with shadow tooling.

consoleSims.title: Provision the catalog database
consoleSims.brief: The software catalog needs its backing store: create the database, its service identity, least-privilege grants, and the first backup.

tasks.instruction: Create a database user named catalog-svc.
tasks.hint: Users & grants section: create user catalog-svc.

tasks.instruction: Grant SELECT on service-catalog to catalog-svc.
tasks.hint: Users & grants section: db service-catalog, user catalog-svc, privilege SELECT.
Databases section: click Back up on service-catalog.

consoleSims.debrief: Platform data stores get the same discipline as the platform: dedicated database, service identity with least privilege, and a backup before the first real write.

consoleSims.title: Ship the platform API
consoleSims.brief: Deploy the platform API itself: its own namespace, pinned image, and a stable service for all the automation clients.

tasks.instruction: Deploy platform-api (image registry.internal/platform-api:1.2.0, 3 replicas) into platform.
tasks.hint: Deployments section: name platform-api, namespace platform, image registry.internal/platform-api:1.2.0, 3 replicas.

tasks.instruction: Expose platform-api on port 80 as a ClusterIP service.
tasks.hint: Services section: deployment platform-api, port 80, type ClusterIP.

consoleSims.debrief: The platform is a workload too: isolated namespace, pinned image, declared service. Dogfooding the golden path is how the platform team finds its own friction.

consoleSims.title: Publish the golden path
consoleSims.brief: Publish the new golden-path release: configure the path version, rebuild the pipeline, and approve the promotion.

tasks.instruction: Set the pipeline variable GOLDEN_PATH to web-service-v2.
tasks.hint: Variables section: key GOLDEN_PATH, value web-service-v2.

tasks.instruction: Trigger a new build of the golden path.
tasks.hint: Pipeline section: click Trigger new build.

tasks.instruction: Approve the gated deploy stage to publish.
tasks.hint: Pipeline section: click Approve on the deploy stage.

consoleSims.debrief: Golden paths ship like products: versioned, built by pipeline, promoted through a gate. The paved road is maintained — that's what makes it paved.

consoleSims.title: Review the template consolidation PR
consoleSims.brief: The template consolidation is proposed as a PR. Work the collaboration loop: branch, propose, merge.

tasks.instruction: Open a PR titled 'Consolidate web service templates' from templates/web-v2 into main.
tasks.hint: Pull requests section: title, base main, head templates/web-v2.
Pull requests section: click Merge on PR #2 (your new PR).

consoleSims.debrief: Platform changes are proposed, not imposed: the consolidation PR lets teams see the parameterized template before it becomes their default. Review is how paved roads get built.

terminalMissions.title: Survey the platform workspace
terminalMissions.brief: Platform work starts with orientation: list the workspace to see what the platform team works with.
terminalMissions.success_message: Platform workspace surveyed. Know the terrain.

terminalMissions.title: Confirm the platform identity
terminalMissions.brief: Platform automation runs as service identities; you're the human. Confirm which user this session is.

terminalMissions.title: Anchor the catalog path
terminalMissions.brief: Catalog tooling uses relative paths. Print the working directory to anchor them.

terminalMissions.title: Record the platform node
terminalMissions.brief: The IDP runs on nodes; record this node's kernel string for the platform baseline.
objectives: Print full kernel and machine information

terminalMissions.title: Name the platform host
terminalMissions.brief: Every host in the platform fleet has a name. Print this one's.

terminalMissions.title: Verify the builder context
terminalMissions.brief: Golden-path templates execute with your identity. Check your user and group context.
objectives: Print user and group identity details

terminalMissions.title: Announce the golden path
terminalMissions.brief: Ship the announcement: echo the golden-path release where the record shows it.
terminalMissions.success_message: Golden path announced: ready. Paved roads get users.

behavioral.prompt: Tell me about the most technically difficult problem you have run into — a homelab, a broken environment, anything — and how you solved it.
points: Pick ONE problem with a real evidence trail: the symptom, what you measured, the hypothesis you tested
Show the loop: scope, observe, hypothesize, smallest safe change, validate — interviewers score the method, not just the fix
Name the tools (VM build, networking, logs) and the lesson it taught you
Close with the result in concrete terms: what works now that did not before
pitfalls: Choosing a story with no real obstacle (“I Googled it” is not a story)
Skipping validation — saying it worked without proving it
Rambling past two minutes without reaching the result

behavioral.prompt: Tell me about a time you dealt with a frustrated customer or user while something was broken.
points: Lead with empathy and ownership: acknowledge the impact before the technical detail
Show translation: what you told them, in their language, plus the timeline you committed to
Show judgment: the narrow fix you chose and what you refused to do (e.g., disabling the control to clear the symptom)
Close with the relationship outcome, not just the technical one
pitfalls: Badmouthing the customer to sound decisive
Promising a timeline you could not keep
Framing the user as the problem rather than the situation

points: Connect prevention to something concrete: a moment you saw detection arrive too late, or a system you hardened
Tie their model to your instincts: deny-by-default matches how you already think about trust
Show service orientation: the Cyber Hero culture rewards the 2 a.m. helper — give an example of being one
Name one forward-looking reason: Zero Trust, the MSP mission, or the bootcamp community investment
pitfalls: Generic flattery with no specifics about the company
Leading with compensation, title, or location convenience
Claiming expertise in products you have only read about — frame it as studied, not mastered
Staying vague ('I analyzed the data') instead of naming what you connected.
Skipping your own role: what did YOU see that others missed?
No outcome: what changed because you joined the dots?
points: The scattered signals and why nobody had connected them yet
The specific links you drew between them (shared host, time, infrastructure)
What the bigger picture turned out to be and what action it drove
What the experience taught you about investigating
behavioral.prompt: Tell me about a time you connected scattered clues into a bigger picture that others had missed.

pitfalls: Claiming you fixed everything: credibility comes from trade-offs, not heroics.
Hiding the constraint: the limitation is what makes the prioritization story real.
No metric: 'better' needs a before-and-after.
points: The constraint (time, budget, staff) and the size of the backlog
How you decided what mattered most (what was reachable, what was critical)
What you did first and what you deliberately deferred
The measurable result of the prioritization
behavioral.prompt: Describe a time you had to prioritize risks or fixes with limited time or resources. How did you decide what came first?

pitfalls: Reciting jargon to a non-technical audience and calling it communication.
Skipping the audience's reaction: did they actually understand and act?
Making yourself the hero instead of the translator.
points: The technical finding and why it mattered
Who the audience was and what they cared about
How you reframed it (a picture, an analogy, a story)
What decision or action the audience took because they understood
behavioral.prompt: Tell me about a time you explained a complex technical finding to a non-technical audience and it changed a decision.
Tell me about a time you used automation or AI to solve a security problem.
points: The repetitive security task and what it cost in analyst time
The automation or AI approach you built and how you validated it
Measured outcome: time saved, detection gained, false positives changed
pitfalls: Describing the tool but never the validation
No measurable outcome

behavioral.prompt: Describe a time you had to decide whether to trust an automated security decision.
points: The stakes of the automated action and its blast radius
How you verified before acting (or the gate you built)
What happened and what you would automate differently next time
pitfalls: Saying you always trust the tool
No mention of blast radius or reversibility

sections.heading: Company facts (verified)
items: Founded 2017 in Orlando, FL — Danny Jenkins (CEO), Sami Jenkins (COO), John Carolan (QA)
Philosophy: deny-by-default / default-deny — approve known-good, deny the rest
Customers: 70,000+ organizations, sold heavily through the MSP channel
Funding: $190M Series F, July 2026 (Elephant-led); ~730 employees
Interview address: 1901 Summit Tower Blvd, Orlando, FL 32810
Culture: in-office 5 days/week; free lunch; post-offer background + drug screening

sections.heading: Product stack
items: Allowlisting — default-deny execution control for apps, DLLs, scripts, installers
Ringfencing — constrains allowed apps: app-to-app, file, registry, network
Storage Control — USB/device policy by serial, user, file type, encryption
Elevation Control — just-in-time per-app admin, no standing rights
Network Control — host firewall; port/IP/dynamic-ACL rules; ZTNA foundation
Web Control — agent-based DNS/URL category filtering, works off-network
Cyber Hero MDR — 24/7/365 US-based response, ~60-second average
Testing Environment — one-button VDI sandbox; checks AV flags, canary files, registry changes

sections.heading: Rule strength (strongest to weakest)
items: Certificate/publisher rules — survive version updates
Hash rules — precise but break on every new version
Path rules — weakest; never in user-writable locations
Learning Mode catalogs before enforcement; Installation Mode pauses blocking — scope and time-box both

sections.heading: Terminal evidence commands
items: nmap <host> — which ports answer (22/80/443 open)
dig <name> — ANSWER SECTION with the A record
ss — listening sockets
systemctl status <svc> — unit state
journalctl -u <svc> — service logs
sha256sum <file> — real SHA-256 identity
grep <pattern> <file> — search the record
ps — what is actually running

sections.heading: Graph vocabulary
items: node — any entity tracked in the model (user, host, IP, domain, file hash, vulnerability)
edge — a labeled relationship between two nodes (logged into, resolved to, downloaded)
degree — number of edges on a node; high-degree nodes are attacker highways
centrality — how much traffic or how many paths flow through a node
directed edge — a relationship with a direction (A downloaded FROM B)
security graph — the living model of your whole environment as nodes and edges
attack graph — the subgraph of exploitable paths to your targets
knowledge graph — threat-intel indicators linked to campaigns and actors

sections.heading: Attack-graph playbook
items: inventory first — you cannot graph what you have not discovered
model flaws AND misconfigs as exploit edges
compute shortest paths to the crown jewels
find the choke point (highest betweenness on those paths)
break the path: patch, segment, or remove the edge
re-scan and re-run the graph to prove the path is gone
never trust yesterday's graph — redeployments redraw the map

sections.heading: Zero Trust + graphs
items: never trust, always verify — re-evaluate every access decision
assume breach — treat unexpected edges as hostile until proven otherwise
microsegmentation — allow-list approved edges, alert on new ones
ReBAC — policies are path queries on the identity graph
continuous verification — device/location/behavior edges change, trust follows
anomalous edge — a first-seen connection between strangers is the classic signal

sections.heading: ML detection vocabulary
items: Supervised learning — learns from labeled examples; strong on known threats, blind to novel ones
Unsupervised learning — finds structure without labels; clustering and dimensionality reduction
Anomaly detection — models 'normal' and flags deviations; the workhorse for novel threats
UEBA — user and entity behavior analytics: per-user baselines plus peer-group comparison
Feature engineering — encoding raw logs into model inputs (login velocity, rare processes, domain entropy)
Concept drift — model decay as attacker behavior and legitimate traffic shift over time

sections.heading: Detection metrics
items: Precision — of all flagged alerts, how many were real
Recall — of all real attacks, how many were flagged
Threshold tuning — sliding the decision cutoff trades precision against recall
Alert fatigue — when false positives train analysts to ignore the queue
DGA — domain generation algorithm; detected via character entropy of domain names

sections.heading: Agent and LLM security
items: Direct prompt injection — attacker input overrides app instructions (OWASP LLM01:2025, the #1 LLM risk)
Indirect prompt injection — hidden instructions inside retrieved data (email, web, docs)
Jailbreak — defeating the model's own safety policy; distinct from hijacking app behavior
Tool poisoning — malicious tool descriptions or metadata steer an agent to misuse its tools (MCP ecosystem risk)
Insecure output handling — executing or trusting model output without validation
Least-privilege tools — grant each tool only the scope its task requires

sections.heading: Adversarial ML and governance
items: Evasion — perturbing inputs at inference time to dodge a classifier
Poisoning — corrupting training data to corrupt the model
Extraction — querying a model to steal its behavior or parameters
MITRE ATLAS — knowledge base of adversarial ML tactics and techniques
Red-teaming and evals — adversarial testing of AI systems before deployment
Human-in-the-loop — required approval for high-impact or irreversible agent actions
SOAR — security orchestration, automation and response; automate enrichment, gate containment

glossary.def: Default-deny execution control: only explicitly approved applications, scripts, and installers may run.
Default-allow model: everything runs except recognized-bad items — the window zero-days live in.
Deny-by-default posture: unknown code, devices, or connections are refused unless explicitly approved.
Containment applied on top of allowlisting; restricts what a permitted app may do across app-to-app, file, registry, and network dimensions.
Agent mode that catalogs applications and dependencies and auto-builds policies before enforcement; temporarily disables file blocking.
Temporary mode that pauses file blocking for installs — must be tightly scoped and time-boxed.
Grants specific approved applications admin rights for standard users — just-in-time, per-app, time-boxed — without standing admin rights.
An elevated or trusted process spawning another tool (e.g., PowerShell) to inherit its privileges — countered by ringfencing the elevated process.
Device and path policy: USB approved by serial, user, file type, time, and encryption; unapproved devices do not connect.
Centrally managed host firewall; rules by port, source IP, and dynamic ACLs; egress allowlisting pins apps to approved destinations.
Zero Trust Network Access: per-session, per-application brokered connections (commonly over port 443) with no open inbound ports — deny-by-default for network access.
Portal queue where end-user software requests arrive for admin review and decision.
Real-time audit showing what was allowed or denied across endpoints — and why; the evidence layer for triage.
One-button cloud VDI sandbox launched from an approval request; logs AV flags, canary-file access, and registry/system changes.
24/7/365 US-based managed detection and response team; validates alerts, isolates hosts, acts on customer runbooks; ~60-second average response.
Design and operate as if the attacker already has a foothold — least privilege, containment, and monitoring everywhere.
Attacks that hijack trusted built-in tools (Word, PowerShell) instead of dropping malware — defeated by behavior containment, not signatures.
Scoped, ticketed, tested changes with validation and rollback — emergency speed never cancels the process.
A node in an attack graph representing a system or weakness, connected by edges that represent steps an attacker could take between them.
How central a node is to paths through the graph (for example, betweenness: how many shortest paths cross it).
The most valuable assets in the environment (customer data, finance systems, source code): what attack paths are measured against.
A labeled connection between two nodes, representing a relationship such as 'logged into' or 'resolved to'.
A graph of threat indicators (IPs, domains, hashes) linked to campaigns, actors, and each other through shared infrastructure.
The practice of mapping relationships in data to reveal hidden associations; rooted in Euler's 1736 graph theory, 1970s paper link charts, and post-2001 intelligence work.
A segment of the network so small that its allowed communications can be enumerated as a graph of approved edges.
An entity in the graph: a user, host, IP address, domain, file, or vulnerability.
Access control where policy is evaluated by traversing relationships on a graph (for example: user reports_to manager who owns the resource's project).
A machine-learning model that operates directly on graph structure to classify nodes or subgraphs, for example labeling attack vs normal behavior.
Monitoring user and entity behavior by modeling their normal relationship patterns and flagging structural anomalies.
ML trained on labeled examples; classifies new inputs into known categories.
ML approach that models normal behavior and flags statistically rare deviations.
Turning raw telemetry into numeric model inputs, e.g. login velocity or domain entropy.
Share of flagged alerts that were real; the false-positive economics of the queue.
Share of real attacks the detector flagged; the miss rate's complement.
Decay of model performance as the data distribution shifts over time.
Attacker-crafted instructions that override an LLM application's intended behavior; direct (user input) or indirect (retrieved data).
Crafted input that defeats an LLM's own safety policy or refusal behavior.
Malicious tool descriptions or metadata that manipulate an AI agent into misusing its tools.
Failing to validate LLM output before acting on it, e.g. executing generated commands.
Adversarial ML technique: perturbing inputs to cross a classifier's decision boundary.
Adversarial Threat Landscape for AI Systems; MITRE's knowledge base of AI attack tactics.
Security orchestration, automation and response; playbooks that enrich automatically and gate containment on humans.
Required human approval before high-impact or irreversible automated actions.

checklist: Sixty-second company brief rehearsed out loud: year, city, philosophy, three products, one milestone
Two STAR stories ready: hardest technical problem; a frustrated customer or user
“Why ThreatLocker / why cybersecurity” answer tied to prevention and service, not slogans
Ringfencing explained in one plain-English sentence (the Word-on-a-leash version)
Elevation Control answer ready: just-in-time, per-app, time-boxed, ringfenced, logged
Triage loop memorized: scope → observe → hypothesize → smallest safe change → validate → explain
Three questions to ask them: team on-call shape, approval SLA expectations, what “most helpful” looks like on the team
Logistics: 1901 Summit Tower Blvd, Orlando FL; in-office role; ID and references ready
Define your crown jewels before you model anything.
Build the asset-and-access graph from live sources (scans, configs, identity), not from the CMDB alone.
Model vulnerabilities AND misconfigurations as exploit edges.
Compute shortest attack paths to each crown jewel; name the choke points.
Prioritize remediation by path risk, not by raw severity score.
Express at least one access policy as a relationship path (ReBAC pilot).
Baseline approved communication edges per segment; alert on first-seen edges.
Brief the next incident or risk review with the graph, not a spreadsheet.
Can you explain supervised vs unsupervised vs anomaly detection with a security example for each?
Can you name three log features you would engineer for a C2 detector and why?
Can you walk through a UEBA alert (baseline, deviation, verification) end to end?
Can you explain the precision/recall tradeoff and how you would set a threshold for a fatigued SOC?
Can you define concept drift and describe a retraining process?
Can you distinguish direct vs indirect prompt injection and jailbreaking?
Can you explain tool poisoning in the MCP ecosystem and three controls against it?
Can you describe insecure output handling and how you would validate agent output?
Can you name the three adversarial ML attack classes and one defense for evasion?
Can you design a SOAR playbook gate: what automates freely, what needs human approval?

media.title: Allowlisting vs blocklisting: default-deny vs default-allow
media.caption: Default-deny stops unknown code without a signature; default-allow runs it until one exists.
media.alt: Side-by-side comparison: on the left, a default-deny gate runs known-good payroll software and denies unknown ransomware with no signature needed; on the right, a default-allow gate runs both until the ransomware is recognized as bad.

media.title: Ringfencing: four leashes on an allowed application
media.caption: Word stays approved, but it cannot spawn PowerShell, read the credential store, or reach the internet — while opening its document is allowed.
media.alt: An approved Word application inside a dashed containment ring: arrows show PowerShell launch denied, credential-store registry access denied, external network denied, and document file access allowed.

media.title: The Zero Trust endpoint stack
media.caption: Five deny-by-default layers — Allowlisting, Ringfencing, Elevation, Storage, Network — watched by Web Control, the Testing Environment, Unified Audit, and the Cyber Hero MDR team.
media.alt: A vertical stack of five layers from Allowlisting at the foundation up through Ringfencing, Elevation Control, Storage Control, and Network Control, with side boxes for Web Control, Testing Environment, Unified Audit, and Cyber Hero MDR.

media.title: Application-request triage flow
media.caption: Gather evidence first, then branch: trusted gets a scoped rule, unknown goes to the sandbox, malicious gets a documented deny.
media.alt: Flowchart from request arrival through evidence gathering to a decision diamond branching into three outcomes: approve with a scoped rule, detonate in the Testing Environment then ringfence, or deny with documented evidence.
Diagram of four labeled nodes (user, host, file, domain, IP) joined by labeled directed edges such as logged into, downloaded, and resolved to, illustrating graph vocabulary.

media.title: Attack graph: shortest path to the crown jewels

media.alt: Seven kill-chain stages as connected graph nodes: reconnaissance, weaponization, delivery, exploitation, installation, command and control, actions. Three alerts are annotated at delivery, installation, and command and control.
media.caption: Three 'unrelated' alerts, one kill-chain subgraph. Correlate by shared entities, not by severity.

media.caption: Valid credentials are not enough. The graph checks device trust, history, and relationships on every request.

media.caption: How raw telemetry becomes scored alerts: features feed the model, the model scores, analysts triage top-down — and analyst verdicts feed retraining.
